newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians feel bite of Israeli sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians feel bite of Israeli sanctions.

text.p: Palestinians have begun to feel the bite of Israeli economic sanctions imposed after suicide bombings in a Jerusalem market last week, economists and Palestinian officials said on Tuesday.
"We are in the midst of an economic blockade unlike any blockade in recent history," Maher al-Masri, Palestinian minister of economy and trade, told a news conference in the West Bank.
After last Wednesday's suicide attack killed 15 including two Arab bombers, the Jewish state sealed its borders to Palestinians and cut off West Bank cities from each other.

Six days of siege have stopped tens of thousands of Arab workers from reaching their jobs in Israel, paralysed trade, shut down factories, kept farmers from their fields and left produce to rot at checkpoints.

Closures have been Israel's standard response to attacks by militants within its borders and are painfully familiar to Palestinians. The current isolation of West Bank cities has led to severe restrictions on the movement of people and goods.

But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's unprecedented decision to withhold transfer payments owed to the Palestinian Authority to press it to crack down on militants put the PA in an acute financial bind.

"It is a real crisis and we're not exaggerating when we say it is a severe crisis. The remittances from Israel represent 60 percent of the Authority's income," Palestinian Finance Minister Mohammad al-Nashashibi told a Gaza news conference.
"They are trying to extort us," Masri said.

Israel transfers on average 115 million to 120 million shekels ($32.4 million to $33.8 million) a month in customs and value added tax (VAT) payments along with 40 million shekels in petroleum tax receipts to the PA under their 1994 Paris economic protocol.
Israel has at this stage frozen the transfer of 70 million shekels, throwing into the question the Authority's ability to meet its current expenditures and pay public sector salaries.

"There are 80,000 people on the payroll of the Palestinian Authority and these people will be turned into an angry army," Mohammad Shtayeh, director of the Palestinian Economic Council for Development and Reconstruction, told reporters.

Economists and officials put losses due to closure at between $5 million and $9 million per day -- a drop in daily output of some 50 percent -- and say an extended siege threatens to reverse months of cautious economic recovery.
"We're building on about nine months of pretty good economic performance by recent historical standards that may be up for grabs now," Salem Ajluni, a United Nations economist in Gaza, told Reuters.
He said the Palestinian economy had been clawing its way out of a deep depression, on track to meet the International Monetary Fund's 1997 growth estimate of 8.1 percent.
The closure also threatens to reverse international donor efforts which only recently began to shift from emergency job creation programmes to more sustainable development projects.

"As a result of the economic and social hardship brought on by closure, attention and resources are diverted to immediate 'firefighting' measures at the expense of longer term development," said World Bank Deputy Representative Ali Khader.
"Unlike in the recent past, the World Bank is not in possession of any further donor funding that would be available to counter the effects of closure," Khader told reporters.
Palestinians have condemned the Israeli measures as collective punishment and warned Netanyahu that tough sanctions would breed despair and strengthen extremism.
"This economic deterioration certainly won't lead to peace," Shtayeh said.
($= 3.55 shekels)
